topics.title: Algebra: expanding and factorising
topics.hook: Multiply EVERY term inside the bracket by the number outside: no term left behind.
topics.intro: Algebra is about doing the same thing to every term. Expanding multiplies out a bracket; factorising puts one back. Collecting like terms tidies up.
topics.talk: Ask her to expand 4(y − 3) in her head.

topics.title: Equations with x on both sides
topics.hook: Move the smaller x term across to join the bigger one, then solve as usual.
topics.intro: When x appears on both sides, move the smaller x term across first. Then it is an equation you already know how to solve.
topics.talk: I think of a number, treble it and add 4. That is the same as doubling it and adding 9. What is my number?

visual.caption: Move the smaller x term first, then solve as usual.

topics.title: Percentage change and reverse percentages
topics.hook: Always work from the ORIGINAL: 20% off means you pay 80%, so divide by 0.8 to go back.
topics.intro: Shops, banks and newspapers all talk in percentage changes. The trap: a percentage is always OF the original amount.
topics.teach: Explain why a 20% rise followed by a 20% cut does not get you back where you started.
topics.talk: A game is £48 after 20% off. Ask her what it cost before (not £57.60!).

visual.caption: After a 20% rise a coat costs £72. That is 120%: 6 blocks of 20%. One block = £72 ÷ 6 = £12, so the original (100%) was 5 × £12 = £60.

topics.title: Angles in polygons
topics.hook: Interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°; exterior angles always add up to 360°.
topics.intro: Every polygon can be cut into triangles, which is why we can work out its angles. Walking round the outside of any shape, you always turn 360°.
topics.teach: Explain why the interior angles of a hexagon add up to 720°.
topics.talk: Count the sides on a 50p coin. What is each interior angle of a regular heptagon?

visual.caption: Diagonals from one corner cut a polygon into (n − 2) triangles, each 180°. Exterior angles always add up to 360°.

topics.title: Angles in parallel lines
topics.hook: F angles are corresponding (equal), Z angles are alternate (equal), C angles are co-interior (add to 180°).
topics.intro: A line crossing two parallel lines makes eight angles, but only two different sizes. Learn the F, Z and C shapes and you can find any of them.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between corresponding and alternate angles.
topics.talk: Find parallel lines in the room (shelves, window bars) and spot a Z angle.

topics.title: Ratio: three parts, differences and best buys
topics.hook: Best buy: compare the price of the SAME amount, such as pence per 100 g.
topics.intro: Harder ratio problems hide the total: sometimes you are told the difference instead. Best-buy questions are ratio in disguise: compare the price of the same amount.
topics.teach: Explain how you compare value for money between two pack sizes.
topics.talk: In the supermarket, ask her which size of a product is better value per 100 g.

visual.caption: Ratio 5 : 2, and Ali has £15 more. Ali’s 3 extra parts are worth £15, so one part is £5: Ali has £25 and Ben £10.

topics.title: Powers and index laws
topics.hook: Multiplying? Add the powers. Dividing? Subtract them. Power of a power? Multiply them.
topics.intro: Powers are repeated multiplication. Once you see that, the three index laws (add, subtract, multiply the little numbers) are obvious.
topics.talk: How many great-great-grandparents does she have? (2⁴)

topics.title: Straight-line graphs
topics.hook: y = mx + c: m is the steepness (gradient), c is where the line crosses the y-axis.
topics.intro: y = 2x + 3 is a rule connecting x and y. Every point that follows the rule sits on a straight line; the 2 is its steepness and the 3 is where it crosses the y-axis.
topics.teach: Explain what the gradient of a line tells you.
topics.talk: Ask her what y = 3x + 1 gives when x = 10, and when x = −2.

topics.title: Fraction arithmetic: mixed numbers and division
topics.hook: Dividing by a fraction: Keep, Change, Flip (KCF). 3 ÷ ½ = 3 × 2 = 6.
topics.intro: The last fraction skills: adding mixed numbers, and dividing by a fraction (which means flipping it and multiplying).
topics.teach: Explain why dividing by a half is the same as doubling.

visual.caption: 3 ÷ ¼ asks “how many quarters fit into 3?” Four in each whole, so 12. Keep, change, flip: 3 × 4 = 12.

topics.title: Circles: circumference and area
topics.hook: Cherry pie’s delicious: C = πd. Apple pies are too: A = πr².
topics.intro: π is the same for every circle in the universe: the circumference is always a little more than three times the diameter. Two formulas and you can measure any circle.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the formulas for circumference and area.
topics.talk: Measure round a mug with string and across it with a ruler. Divide. Did you get about 3.14?

items.example: 4 lunch bags, each with a sandwich and 2 apples: 4(s + 2a) = 4s + 8a.
Gym A: £20 to join plus £5 a visit. Gym B: £9 a visit. 20 + 5x = 9x, so after 5 visits they cost the same.
A coat costs £60 in a 25% off sale. You pay 75%, so the original price was £60 ÷ 0.75 = £80.
Hexagonal floor tiles fit with no gaps: each angle is 120°, and three of them meet to make 360°.
A five-bar gate: the diagonal bar crosses the parallel bars and makes Z-shaped alternate angles.
Cereal: 500 g for £2 is 40p per 100 g; 750 g for £2.70 is 36p per 100 g, so the big box is better value.
Fold a sheet of paper in half 5 times and you get 2⁵ = 32 layers.
A taxi charges £3 to get in plus £2 a mile: fare = 2 × miles + 3, which is the line y = 2x + 3.
How many quarter-pizzas in 3½ pizzas? 3½ ÷ ¼ = 7/2 × 4 = 14.
A bike wheel 70 cm across rolls about 3.14 × 70 ≈ 220 cm forward on every turn.
